paper_title: RubatoCodec: Budgeted Adaptive Speech Tokenization with Streaming Decoding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Neural speech codecs provide discrete tokens for speech generation. Lower frame rates shorten token sequences, but each token must then carry more linguistic and acoustic information. Variable-frame-rate codecs address this trade-off by adapting token allocation to speech content, but threshold-based allocation lets content determine the token count, so the sequence length a speech generator must produce varies across utterances and datasets at a fixed setting. We present RubatoCodec, a variable-frame-rate speech codec built on X-Codec-2 with an exact utterance-level event budget and streaming decoding. Its Adaptive Firing mechanism uses changes in codec features and waveform spectra to divide speech into variable-duration events without a learned boundary predictor. Discrete codes and an explicit duration represent each event, allowing a speech generator to predict and decode one event at a time. Controlled experiments show that adaptive allocation outperforms fixed-rate coding in reconstruction fidelity and intelligibility at low event rates. A model trained on large-scale multilingual speech achieves competitive reconstruction quality across English, Japanese, and Mandarin, with the best intelligibility preservation among the compared codecs on the evaluated English and Japanese benchmarks at comparable bitrates. In a matched text-to-speech comparison, the adaptive representation yields lower WER and higher UTMOS and UTMOSv2 with comparable speaker similarity. The speech generator also learns the codec's utterance-level event budget without an explicit generation-time rate constraint. These results demonstrate that budgeted adaptive speech representations support both high-quality reconstruction and streaming text-to-speech generation. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec and https://huggingface.co/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Neural speech codecs encode waveforms as discrete tokens for reconstruction [13] and language-model-based generation, including AudioLM [4], VALL-E [5], and recent synthesis and spoken dialogue systems [69]. For generation, the codecs frame rate determines the temporal sequence length: ten seconds of speech requires 500 positions at 50 Hz. Lower rates shorten this sequence but require each position to represent longer acoustic interval. Recent tokenizers operate at 12.5 Hz [6, 8, 9], where each token spans 80 ms. At this resolution, where boundaries fall relative to speech content matters: fixed grid can merge rapid phonetic transition into single token while spending as many tokens on pause as on the transition. Speech is temporally nonstationary: pauses and steady vowels change slowly, whereas transitions change rapidly. Variable-rate representations and variable-frame-rate codecs exploit this by assigning different durations to frames [1015]. Threshold-based allocation, however, lets content determine the frame count, so rates vary

sections.title: Third Intelligence
sections.content: across utterances and datasets at fixed setting [14, 15]. For example, one released threshold-based codec ranges from 46.1 to 81.5 events/s under single threshold across our five evaluation datasets (Section 5.4.1). Calibrating the threshold on representative data can match an average rate, but it neither fixes the count for an individual utterance nor preserves that average when the data distribution shifts. Sequence length, and with it downstream modeling cost, then cannot be determined from audio duration alone. An explicit event budget removes this dependence: placement adapts to content, while utterance duration determines the sequence length. Prescribed-count segmentation has been explored in codecs and speech representation methods [11, 12, 16]. We build on this principle with codec that uses deterministic firing signal to allocate events, learns duration-aware representations of those events, and decodes them causally. RubatoCodec separates the number of events from their placement. retention ratio 𝑅 fixes the number of events for 𝑇 latent frames at 𝐾 = round(𝑅𝑇) (Section 3.3.2), and Adaptive Firing places them by cumulative allocation of signal derived from latent dissimilarity and waveform spectral flux, without learned boundary predictor. The default 𝑅 = 0.25 yields 12.5 events/s on average from 50-Hz latent grid, with variable event durations. The name reflects the musical term rubato: local timing flexes while the overall tempo is preserved. RubatoCodec builds on X-Codec-2 [7], retaining its acoustic/semantic encoder and spectral synthesis backbone while introducing adaptive aggregation and causal decoding. Each event carries discrete codes and an explicit duration, allowing downstream model to predict and decode completed events incrementally. We evaluate the design through controlled codec comparisons, multilingual reconstruction, and downstream TTS training. Our contributions are: 1. Budgeted content-adaptive speech tokenization. Adaptive Firing combines an exact utterance-level event budget with cumulative allocation driven by latent dissimilarity and waveform spectral flux. An onset-anchored aggregator combines frame features and duration within each event to construct its quantizer input. Event boundaries require neither learned boundary predictor nor rate-penalty optimization. 2. Controlled analysis of adaptive allocation. Matched comparisons show reconstruction gains over fixedrate downsampling at low event rates, and placement-only comparison indicates that content-adaptive boundaries contribute to these gains. We also characterize how event rate and quantizer depth trade off at matched bitrates. 3. codeduration interface for streaming generation. Each event carries semantically supervised codes and an explicit duration, which causal decoder renders as they become available. Large-scale multilingual evaluation shows competitive reconstruction quality, including the best intelligibility preservation among the compared codecs on the evaluated English and Japanese benchmarks at comparable bitrates. In matched TTS training, the representation yields lower WER and higher UTMOS and UTMOSv2 scores with comparable speaker similarity, and the generator learns the codecs utterance-level event budget without an explicit rate constraint.

sections.title: 2.1 Neural speech codecs for language modeling
sections.content: SoundStream and EnCodec combine residual vector quantization with adversarial waveform reconstruction [1, 2]; DAC improves the quantization and reconstruction components [3]. Quantizer depth controls the information carried per temporal position. BigCodec instead studies high-capacity single-codebook representations at low bitrates [17]. Semantic supervision encourages codec tokens to retain linguistic content. SpeechTokenizer supervises the first RVQ layer with self-supervised features [18], while Mimi combines semantically distilled VQ with parallel acoustic RVQ [6]. X-Codec-2 fuses an acoustic encoder with frozen w2v-BERT 2.0 features and uses

sections.title: Third Intelligence
sections.content: semantic reconstruction supervision [7]. RubatoCodec builds on this architecture, including its Vocos-style spectral decoder [19], and adopts the synthesis upsampling approach of Inworld TTS [20]. Low-frame-rate tokenizers reduce the temporal sequence length presented to generative model. Mimi and the publicly released Qwen3-TTS-Tokenizer-12Hz operate at 12.5 Hz with semantic supervision [6, 8], while MOSS-Audio-Tokenizer learns low-rate representation through jointly optimized reconstruction, adversarial, and audio-to-text objectives without an external semantic distillation teacher [9].

sections.title: 2.2 Variable-frame-rate speech coding
sections.content: Early variable-rate discrete representations combine slow autoencoders with run-length coding [10]. Recent codecs adapt temporal resolution through hierarchy selection, merging, or boundary selection. TFC uses waveform-derived temporal entropy and utterance-level granularity ratios [11]; VARSTok clusters contiguous latent frames and encodes duration in token identity [13]; FlexiCodec merges frames using frozen SenseVoice features and adjusts rate through its merge threshold [14]. RubatoCodec constructs its firing signal from fused-latent dissimilarity and waveform spectral flux. CodecSlime constrains segment count through dynamic programming over feature distortion, adapting pretrained fixed-rate codec through its Melt-and-Cool procedure [12]. RubatoCodec instead normalizes its firing signal to the event budget and places boundaries by cumulative firing, without searching candidate segmentations. Its trainable codec components learn from scratch with adaptive allocation active throughout training. Elastic Time augments frozen audio autoencoder with learned latent predictor, using greedy or dynamicprogramming boundary selection to retain target number of anchor frames and reconstruct omitted frames [21]. It adjusts the frame rate of continuous latents at inference; RubatoCodec instead produces discrete codes with explicit durations for causal decoding. DTM-Codecs Path Length Equalization selects boundaries at successive thresholds of accumulated latent change [15]. Its fixed threshold lets total change determine the event count; RubatoCodec normalizes bounded increments to prescribed count. DyCAST uses character alignment or learned boundary predictor and supports transmitted durations, length-conditioned duration prediction, or free duration prediction [22]. Its total-length constraint concerns decoded durations, not the number of encoded events. Adaptive placement, inference-time rate adjustment, and exact event counts are distinct properties. FlexiCodec and DTM-Codec offer threshold-based adjustment; TFC, CodecSlime, and RubatoCodec enforce prescribed counts. The dynamic tokenizer in The WER Trap normalizes frame weights to prescribed token count before soft aggregation and FSQ [16]. It follows Continuous Integrate-and-Fire (CIF), which accumulates learned weights into feature sums and uses target-length normalization during training [23]. Beyond waveform coding, Once-for-All compression extends CIF to inference-time rate adjustment [24], and SpeechCLIP+ combines CIF with vector quantization and input-length-based targets [25]. RubatoCodec shares cumulative budget allocation but separates boundary placement from event representation: deterministic statistics set event boundaries, and an aggregator combines the onset feature, the mean of the enclosed frame features, and the duration for each event. Table 1 compares VFR codecs in terms of temporal allocation, event-count control, timing representation, and training procedure.

sections.title: 3 RubatoCodec Architecture
sections.content: RubatoCodec retains X-Codec-2s acoustic/semantic encoding, feature fusion, semantic reconstruction pathway, and Transformer-based spectral synthesis backbone [7]. We modify the temporal bottleneck through Adaptive Firing, interval aggregation, hybrid residual quantization, and duration-aware grid reconstruction (Figure 1). Causal decoding enables incremental synthesis. RubatoCodec also uses factor-three upsampler inspired by Inworld TTS that raises the synthesis feature rate [20].

sections.title: Third Intelligence
sections.content: The decoder retains the X-Codec-2 Transformer backbone [7], with causal attention and convolutional dependencies. projection maps the 2,048-dimensional grid to this 1,024-dimensional backbone, which uses causal embedding convolution, 12 Transformer layers, rotary positions, and 16 attention heads. factor-three transposed-convolution upsampler, inspired by the super-resolution module in Inworld TTS [20], produces 150-Hz synthesis features. Vocos-style spectral head predicts magnitude and phase, followed by forward-window ISTFT with hop size of 294 samples for 44.1-kHz output [19]. Convolutions are left-padded, transposed convolutions are right-trimmed, and attention excludes future frames, so synthesis depends only on the current and preceding events. The ISTFT places each 1,176-sample synthesis window at the current frames hop position and extends it forward in time. Each frame finalizes the next 294 samples, carrying waveform and window-normalization overlap buffers into subsequent frames. With three synthesis frames per grid step, an event of duration 𝑑𝑖 accounts for 882𝑑𝑖 output samples. At startup, normalization assumes preceding silent windows, yielding 20-ms fade-in; at termination, the remaining window overhang is discarded rather than emitted as additional audio. During inference, the decoder periodically discards its cached states and rebuilds them from window of recent events beginning at an event onset, which limits long-utterance extrapolation. At each such history recomputation, short crossfade blends the audio decoded before and after the recomputation. Streaming decoding processes incoming events incrementally, reusing decoder states between history recomputations and briefly buffering audio for the crossfade.

sections.title: 3.6 Model size and bitrate
sections.content: RubatoCodec contains approximately 246.1M codec parameters: 72.3M in the encoding path, 172.7M in the decoding path, and 1.1M in the quantizer. The additional frozen w2v-BERT 2.0 encoder has approximately 580M parameters, bringing the complete model to approximately 826M. Token-to-waveform synthesis uses the decoding path and quantizer without the encoding components. Each event contains 𝐷 code indices of 12 bits each. For 𝐾 events over represented duration of 𝜏 = 𝑇/50 seconds, the content bitrate is 𝐵content = 12𝐷𝐾 𝜏 . (16) At 12.5 events per second, depths 1, 4, 8, and 16 correspond to content bitrates of 0.15, 0.60, 1.20, and 2.40 kbit/s, respectively. Timing bitrate is estimated from the empirical entropy ˆ𝐻 (𝑑) of event durations, pooled within each evaluation dataset (Section 5.1.2). The estimated total bitrate is 𝐵total = 𝐵content + (𝐾/𝜏) ˆ𝐻 (𝑑).

sections.title: 4 Training Data and Optimization
sections.content: We train adaptive and fixed-rate architectures on shared English subset at 6.25, 12.5, and 25 events/s, and adaptive and uniform-stride models at 12.5 events/s for the placement comparison. We then train multilingual RubatoCodec on larger speech mixture for comparison with external codecs.

sections.title: 4.1 Objectives and phases
sections.content: Both settings combine reconstruction, semantic supervision, quantization, adversarial, and perceptual objectives: L𝐺 = 15Lmel + 5Lsem + LVQ + 1phase2(Ladv + LFM) + 1phase=3Lperc. (17)

sections.title: Third Intelligence
sections.content: Multi-resolution mel reconstruction. Following DAC [3], Lmel sums mean absolute log-mel differences at 44.1 kHz over eight resolutions: window lengths 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, quarter-window hops, and corresponding mel-bin counts 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, 640. Magnitudes are clamped to 105 before the base-10 logarithm. Semantic reconstruction. Equation (14) supervises the first layer with frozen w2v-BERT 2.0 layer-16 features. RubatoCodec evaluates the loss at event starts. For fixed-rate controls, the 50-Hz teacher features are averaged over nonoverlapping groups of 8, 4, or 2 frames to match the 6.25-, 12.5-, or 25-Hz latent grid, respectively. These averaged features serve both as inputs to the semantic encoder for feature fusion and as targets for the semantic loss, which is evaluated at every latent position. Quantization. LVQ sums squared-error commitment and codebook losses over residual VQ layers [3], with weights 0.25 and 1.0 and stop-gradients on the code vector and encoder representation, respectively. FSQ has neither loss [30]. Adversarial training and feature matching. We use HiFi-GANs multi-period discriminator with periods 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 17, 23, 37 [31] and UnivNet-style multi-resolution STFT-magnitude discriminator [32] with FFT/window sizes 216, 348, 568, 920, 1494, 2414, 3908, 6328 and half-window hops. Least-squares GAN losses use target labels one for real audio and zero for reconstructed audio, while the generator targets one [31]. LFM sums mean absolute differences of intermediate activations across both discriminator families, with detached target features. Discriminator parameters remain fixed during generator updates. Perceptual reconstruction. Following Llasas late-stage waveform supervision [7], Lperc compares frozen speech-model features of target and reconstructed audio resampled to 16 kHz. We use wav2vec2-XLS-R-300M [33], averaging mean squared feature error over layers 1021. Gradients propagate through the frozen extractor to the codec. Training phases. The first 10% of updates use mel, semantic, and quantization losses; the next 75% add adversarial and feature-matching losses; the final 15% also use perceptual loss. Trainable codec components start from scratch, while both pretrained feature extractors remain frozen.

sections.title: 4.2 Training for architecture comparisons
sections.content: Fixed-rate controls downsample before quantization to produce uniformly spaced codes. The adaptive architecture retains the 50-Hz grid and aggregates features within variable-duration events, restoring their representations to that grid for decoding. The adaptive-versus-fixed-rate comparisons use the same approximately 5,000-hour English subset of HiFiTTS2s 44-kHz partition [34]. We verified that the full HiFiTTS-2 dataset has no speaker overlap with LibriSpeech test-clean. Models are trained separately at each target event rate for 100,000 steps using aligned six-second crops. Both models use global batch of 64 and the objectives in Section 4.1; detailed training settings are provided in Appendix C.1. The adaptive models use the budget-constrained allocation in Section 3.3.2, with retention ratios of 0.125, 0.25, and 0.5 for nominal event rates of 6.25, 12.5, and 25 Hz. Quantizer configuration, decoder depth and width, output sample rate, losses, and optimization are shared; encoder strides and synthesis upsampling differ to accommodate the temporal grids  (Table 3)  . To isolate the effect of adaptive event placement, we additionally train adaptive and uniform-stride aggregation models on the full English 44-kHz training partition of HiFiTTS-2 for one million steps, using nominal event rate of 12.5 Hz. Both retain the same 50-Hz encoder and decoder grids, interval aggregator, and hybrid residual quantizer. The uniform control forms four-frame events. The global batch remains 64. The firing-signal, decoder-causality, grid-composition, and firing-rule ablations are described in Appendix A.

sections.title: 4.3 Multilingual model training
sections.content: The multilingual model is trained on approximately 375,000 hours of public and internal speech data. Public sources include Emilia-YODAS (English, Japanese, Chinese, German, French, and Korean) [35], the 44-kHz subset of HiFiTTS-2 [34], ReazonSpeech [36], The Peoples Speech (excluding ShareAlike-licensed data) [37], VoxPopuli [38], Multilingual LibriSpeech (excluding English) [39], Omnilingual ASR Corpus [40], and IndicVoices [41]. Combined with internal data, the mixture covers read, spontaneous, conversational, broadcast, and expressive speech. English, Japanese, and Chinese account for approximately 44%, 27%, and 13% of the training data, respectively, with other languages making up the remaining 16%. Waveforms are resampled to 16 kHz for encoding and 44.1 kHz for reconstruction targets, with aligned six-second random crops; shorter examples are zero-padded. The multilingual model uses retention ratio 0.25 and is trained for 1.5 million steps with global batch of 160, following the loss phases in Section 4.1. Optimization settings and loss schedules are detailed in Appendix C.1.

sections.title: 5.1.1 Datasets
sections.content: We evaluate speech reconstruction on five datasets covering English, Japanese, and Mandarin Chinese, with 10,563 utterances in total  (Table 4)  . The adaptive-versus-fixed comparisons use LibriSpeech test-clean, while the multilingual model and external codecs are evaluated across all five datasets. For VCTK, we use the silence-trimmed mic1 recordings and retain utterances with nonempty transcripts and durations between 1 and 40 seconds. We then randomly select 12 eligible utterances per speaker, yielding 1,308 utterances from 109 speakers. The same subset is used for all codecs.

sections.title: 5.1.2 Metrics
sections.content: Reconstruction-quality metrics use audio resampled to 16 kHz. Event rate and bitrate. We compute event rate and bitrate per utterance using the duration represented by the codecs temporal grid, and report their arithmetic means within each dataset. Event rate is the number of encoded events per second; for fixed-rate codecs, each frame counts as one event. Bitrate includes code-index and timing costs (Section 3.6). Explicit timing symbols are assigned their dataset-pooled empirical entropy per symbol; timing embedded in token indices is included in the code-index cost.

sections.title: 5.2.1 Adaptive versus fixed-rate architectures
sections.content: We compare the adaptive architecture with fixed-rate downsampling controls on LibriSpeech test-clean under the matched training conditions in Section 4.2. The architectures differ in temporal aggregation, latent-grid resolution, and decoder upsampling factors  (Table 3)  . Comparison at 12.5 Hz At the default event rate of 12.5 Hz, the adaptive codec additionally transmits event durations, which add approximately 0.028 kbit/s to the reported bitrate  (Table 6)  . At both depths, the adaptive codec improves every metric except SIM  (Table 6)  . The gains grow with depth: PESQ-WB rises by 0.057 at depth 8 and by 0.114 at depth 16, where dWER falls from 0.72% to 0.62%. SIM is lower by 0.019 and 0.003, respectively. The intelligibility advantage extends to single-codebook reconstruction, where dWER falls from 16.86% to 14.41% (Figure 3). These gains reflect the combined effects of interval aggregation, adaptive placement, and decoding on 50-Hz grid, compared with the controls 12.5-Hz grid. Comparisons at 6.25 and 25 Hz We also compare separately trained models at 6.25 and 25 Hz, using retention ratios 𝑅 = 0.125 and 𝑅 = 0.5 and one seed per configuration  (Table 7)  . At 6.25 Hz, the pattern matches 12.5 Hz: the adaptive codec improves every metric except SIM at both depths  (Table 7)  , most clearly at depth 16 (PESQ-WB 1.812 1.932, dWER 1.24% 1.08%). At 25 Hz, the difference narrows. The adaptive codec keeps higher UTMOSv2 and DNSMOS at both depths and higher PESQ-WB and STOI at depth 16, but the fixed-rate control has slightly lower dWER at both depths (0.52% versus 0.53% and 0.45% versus 0.47%) and higher SIM at depth 8, with equal SIM at depth 16. sections.title: 5.2.3 Event rate and quantizer depth at similar bitrates
sections.content: Table 9 compares adaptive operating points with code-index rates of 1.2 or 2.4 kbit/s, trading event rate against quantizer depth. Total bitrates additionally include duration information. Near 1.2 kbit/s, 12.5 Hz at depth 8 nearly matches 25 Hz at depth 4 in PESQ-WB (2.379 versus 2.387), with slightly lower dWER (0.80% versus 0.84%) and higher UTMOSv2, but lower SIM (0.757 versus 0.771). At 6.25 Hz, even depth 16 falls well behind in fidelity and SIM. Near 2.4 kbit/s, 25 Hz at depth 8 is clearly ahead of 12.5 Hz at depth 16 (PESQ-WB 2.815 versus 2.556), with only UTMOSv2 favoring 12.5 Hz. The 12.5-Hz configuration thus halves the temporal sequence length relative to 25 Hz at nearly the same signal fidelity and intelligibility near 1.2 kbit/s. Hierarchical generators can trade temporal-backbone steps for codebook predictions in lighter within-event module [6, 8, 56]; Section 7.2 discusses this trade-off. We also vary the retention ratio at inference for the multilingual model trained at 12.5 Hz, without retraining. Higher event rates improve reconstruction fidelity and speaker similarity, whereas substantial rate reductions sharply degrade quality even at greater quantizer depths (Appendix A.5).

sections.title: 6.2 TTS evaluation
sections.content: We compare TTS using the 100,000-update adaptive and fixed-rate codecs from Section 4.2, both with eight quantizer layers. Each encodes approximately 31,300 hours from HiFiTTS-2s English 44-kHz partition after reserving held-out speakers [34]. Both TTS models are trained for three epochs with Qwen3-0.6B temporal backbone and four-layer local Transformer, using matched initialization and training settings (Appendix C.2). For adaptive coding, utterances containing durations above 64 frames (1.28 s) are excluded, affecting approximately 0.07% of training utterances. We evaluate zero-shot voice cloning on the 1,088 English utterances in seed-tts-eval [46], using the same target texts and reference recordings for both systems. Following the benchmark protocol, WER is computed from Whisper-large-v3 transcriptions [47], and SIM is the cosine similarity of embeddings from the same fine-tuned WavLM-Large speaker verification model [53] between generated speech and the original reference recording. We additionally assess predicted speech quality with UTMOS [58] and UTMOSv2 [51]. Sampling settings are listed in Appendix C.2. TTS WER is macro-averaged over utterances, following the seed-tts-eval protocol; SIM, UTMOS, and UTMOSv2 are also averaged over utterances. The adaptive codec achieves lower WER and comparable speaker similarity, with higher UTMOS and UTMOSv2 scores  (Table 18)  .

sections.title: 7.1 Adaptive allocation under an explicit budget
sections.content: An exact event budget leaves useful freedom to distribute temporal resolution within an utterance. This freedom matters most at lower event rates: the gains over fixed-rate downsampling appear at 6.25 and 12.5 Hz and narrow at 25 Hz (Section 5.2.1). Those comparisons change placement, interval aggregation, and decoding grid together, and the adaptive codec has lower speaker similarity there. With aggregation and grid held fixed, however, adaptive placement raises speaker similarity relative to uniform stride (Section 5.2.2). Although the two comparisons use different training data and lengths, this suggests that the SIM gap in Section 5.2.1 stems from interval aggregation and grid design rather than from placement itself. The uniform-stride comparison (Section 5.2.2) supports content-dependent event placement with aggregation and decoding grid held fixed. The firing-rule comparison (Appendix A.4) separately favors cumulative allocation over the tested level-thresholding rule. Cumulative allocation produces approximately uniform spacing under constant firing signal and adjusts that spacing with the cumulative bounded increments. Broad temporal coverage combined with content-dependent placement is one possible explanation for its performance, but these experiments do not isolate that mechanism. The firing analysis shows how the budget is used: events longer than 300 ms predominantly cover low-energy regions across all five datasets, leaving more events for the remaining speech (Section 5.4.2). Budgeted and threshold-based allocation also make different trade-offs. prescribed count gives predictable sequence lengths without dataset-specific calibration, but equally long utterances receive the same budget regardless of acoustic complexity. Threshold-based methods can instead spend more events on difficult utterances.

sections.title: 7.2 Temporal resolution and quantizer depth for speech generation
sections.content: Temporal resolution and quantizer depth are not interchangeable ways of spending bitrate budget. In the evaluated configurations, additional residual layers do not fully compensate for coarser segmentation: 12.5 Hz approaches 25 Hz near 1.2 kbit/s, but 6.25 Hz falls clearly behind, and 25 Hz regains fidelity advantage near 2.4 kbit/s (Section 5.2.3). For generation, these choices also distribute computation differently. Hierarchical models such as Moshi, Qwen3-TTS, and MOSS-TTS predict codebook tokens with smaller within-event module [6, 8, 56]. Increasing depth adds predictions there, whereas increasing event rate adds steps to the larger temporal backbone. The reconstruction results therefore motivate 12.5 Hz as practical compromise between quality and sequence length, without establishing it as optimal. Because RubatoCodecs waveform decoder still operates on 50-Hz grid, the shorter sequence reduces downstream modeling cost but not waveform-decoder computation. The inference-time ratio experiment (Appendix A.5) shows asymmetric tolerance to event rates outside the training setting: raising the rate improves reconstruction at additional bitrate, whereas aggressive reduction degrades it sharply even at greater quantizer depth. The model thus tolerates higher, but not lower, inference rates.

sections.title: 7.3 From encoded durations to generated timing
sections.content: The matched TTS comparison shows that codes and durations can be generated jointly while improving intelligibility and predicted quality over the fixed-rate codec (Section 6.2). Each completed event can be passed directly to the causal waveform decoder, so the same representation serves both temporal compression and incremental synthesis. The generator also learns the codecs utterance-level event budget. Generated event counts match the codecs budget rule for 88.3% of utterances and fall within one event for 99.9% (Section 6.3), so the generator offsets long events with short ones within each utterance. Generated sequence length therefore remains predictable,

sections.title: Third Intelligence
sections.content: although no rate constraint is imposed during generation. Long events also predominantly correspond to low-energy regions in both encoded speech and generated audio under the same measurement criterion (Sections 5.4.2 and 6.3), indicating that the generator reproduces the codecs use of long events for near-silence. The concentration of long events at utterance boundaries is consistent with learning leading and trailing silence from HiFiTTS-2, although that training-data correspondence has not been measured directly. Pause placement, however, is not always natural: informal listening revealed an unnatural within-phrase pause associated with long event (Section 6.3). Efficiently representing silence and placing pauses naturally are therefore distinct modeling concerns.

sections.title: 7.4 Reconstruction quality and multilingual performance
sections.content: On the English benchmarks, RubatoCodec combines strong intelligibility preservation with high predictedquality scores, while the strongest comparators retain higher signal fidelity and speaker similarity (Section 5.3). On the Japanese benchmarks, its intelligibility advantage extends to both read and emotional speech, whereas predicted-quality rankings depend on the dataset. In Mandarin, intelligibility preservation remains competitive, although the strongest alternatives achieve lower dCER. These patterns distinguish preservation of linguistic content, speaker characteristics, and waveform detail; improvements in one need not imply improvements in the others. RubatoCodecs UTMOSv2 scores exceed those of the original recordings on LibriSpeech, indicating that higher predicted quality should not be interpreted as greater fidelity to the source. The 44.1-kHz output rate is synthesis capability, not evidence of full-band source recovery. Encoding uses 16-kHz input, so higher frequencies must be inferred. The English, Japanese, and Mandarin results establish reconstruction across languages with shared model and allocation rule. Combined with the cross-dataset rate analysis (Section 5.4.1), they demonstrate both predictable encoded sequence lengths and content preservation across the evaluated languages.

sections.title: 7.5 Scope and limitations
sections.content: The reported architecture comparisons use one trained model per configuration, and supporting architectural ablations have narrower coverage. In particular, firing-signal selection uses an early single-FSQ, low-bitrate design and smaller training budget; its ranking may change with the current residual quantizer and training scale (Appendix A.1). The placement comparison uses one seed and English read speech, so its robustness across training runs, languages, and recording conditions remains untested. Firing statistics characterize duration and energy associations, not phonetic alignment or optimal allocation, and do not separate the quality contribution of allocation within speech from that of allocation to low-energy regions. External codecs differ in training resources and operating points. Reporting realized rates and timing costs makes these differences visible but does not control them. All evaluated languages occur in RubatoCodecs training mixture, so the multilingual results do not establish unseen-language transfer or language robustness attributable solely to Adaptive Firing. Dataset differences also confound language, speakers, and recording conditions. TTS evidence covers one English audiobook corpus and codecs from the controlled comparison (Section 4.2). The comparison evaluates the complete representation and does not isolate the TTS contribution of adaptive placement. It also does not establish the quality attainable with the multilingual codec, broader data, or larger generator. Long events are more frequent in TTS than in the reconstruction evaluation, but the corpora differ. Human evaluation remains necessary to assess reconstruction and TTS preferences and pause naturalness.

sections.title: Third Intelligence
sections.content: For the codec, the priority is signal fidelity at low event rates: how far improved acoustic representations and reconstruction objectives can close PESQ/STOI gaps without longer sequences, and when finer temporal resolution becomes necessary. Training with multiple retention ratios could broaden the inference-time tolerance observed in Appendix A.5, following adjustable-rate coding and sequence compression [14, 24]. Online encoding would further require causal acousticsemantic path and windowed or running budget in place of the utterance-level guarantee, trading buffering latency against placement quality and rate control. For generation, larger-scale TTS with the multilingual codec, broader data, and larger backbones would test whether reconstruction improvements carry over, and explicit durations could support utterance-length and pause control. Finally, applying Adaptive Firing to other codec backbones and to music or environmental sound would test its generality.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced RubatoCodec, speech codec that combines content-adaptive event placement, an exact utterance-level event budget, and streaming waveform decoding. By representing speech as discrete codes paired with durations, it allows temporal resolution to follow speech content while keeping sequence length predictable. Controlled experiments support the value of adaptive allocation for reconstruction at low event rates. Multilingual evaluation demonstrates competitive reconstruction quality, with the best intelligibility preservation among the compared codecs on the evaluated English and Japanese benchmarks at comparable bitrates. Signal fidelity remains an area for improvement relative to the strongest alternatives. In matched text-to-speech experiments, the adaptive representation improves intelligibility and predicted speech quality with comparable speaker similarity. The generator also learns the codecs utterance-level event budget without an explicit rate constraint. These results support budgeted adaptive speech tokenization as practical representation for both reconstruction and speech generation. Combining content-dependent timing with predictable sequence length provides basis for compact speech modeling and streaming synthesis.

sections.content: A.1 Firing-signal selection We conducted this preliminary study before introducing residual vector quantization, using single FSQ codebook to compare candidate firing signals (Table A1). Each model was trained for 100,000 steps and evaluated on 200 utterances from HiFiTTS-2 validation split constructed by holding out speakers from the training subset. The scores serve primarily to compare signal choices within this early configuration; their absolute values do not characterize the final codec and are not directly comparable with the LibriSpeech test-clean results in Section 5.2.1. Latent dissimilarity and flux. Multi-scale latent dissimilarity and waveform flux are the two components described in Section 3.3.1: the latent-dissimilarity component in Equation (5) and log-mel spectral flux in Equation (6). Adjacent latent dissimilarity is the single-offset variant of Equation (5), using only (𝑎, 𝑏) = (1, 0), so it compares each latent frame with its immediate predecessor. The multi-scale-plus-flux row uses the firing signal defined in Equation (3). Learned difficulty. separate convolutional network takes the current and preceding latent frames and predicts nonnegative scalar reconstruction difficulty. During training, its target is the decoders framewise absolute log-mel reconstruction error, averaged over mel bins and normalized by its utterance mean. The network learns this target with mean-squared regression loss; during encoding, its prediction supplies the firing signal without requiring waveform reconstruction. In mixed-signal variants, each component is normalized to unit utterance mean before summation. We prioritize firing signals that require no additional trainable predictor. Among these candidates, multi-scale latent dissimilarity combined with spectral flux achieves the highest PESQ-WB, with STOI and speaker similarity comparable to flux alone, although dWER is slightly higher. Learned difficulty combined with flux yields lower dWER but requires an additional predictor and has lower speaker similarity. We therefore adopt the combined firing signal as balance between architectural simplicity and reconstruction quality in this exploratory comparison. A.2 Effect of causal decoding We compared the fully causal decoder architecture described in Section 3.5 with fully non-causal variant, keeping the rest of the codec architecture unchanged, at 12.5 events per second. The non-causal variant uses bidirectional attention, symmetric padding in its convolutional and transposed-convolutional layers, and symmetrically cropped overlap-add synthesis in the ISTFT. sections.title: B Duration Prediction Order
sections.content: This ablation compares four ways to predict event duration alongside codebook tokens. The independent-head variant predicts continuation, duration, and the first codebook token through three separate heads at the first local Transformer position; the remaining codes are predicted autoregressively without conditioning on the current duration. The other variants insert duration into the local autoregressive sequence before all codes, after the first (semantically supervised) code, or after all codes (Table B1). Duration is conditioned on preceding codes, and subsequent codes are conditioned on duration. The duration-last variant corresponds to Equation (18). All four models share Qwen3-0.6B temporal backbone [57], single-layer local Transformer, eight codebooks, and the same frozen codec. Each is trained for 20,000 steps on approximately 4,000 hours from the HiFiTTS-2 44-kHz subset [34], with global batch of 128 and training seed 42. AdamW [59] uses learning rates of 104 for the pretrained backbone and 3 104 for newly initialized modules, with 1,000 warmup steps followed by cosine decay. Reference speech is supplied with probability 0.9 and limited to 375 events. We evaluate duration cross-entropy on HiFiTTS-2 validation split with speakers held out from TTS training, and TTS WER on the 1,088 English utterances in seed-tts-eval [46]. Duration cross-entropy is not directly comparable across orders: duration-last conditions on all current-event codes, which may retain duration information from interval aggregation (Equation (12)). Its lower cross-entropy therefore reflects easier prediction under this conditioning rather than better modeling of temporal structure. We adopt duration-last prediction based on its lower duration cross-entropy and TTS WER in this small-scale comparison (Table B1).

sections.title: C Training Settings
sections.content: C.1 Codec training Table C1 provides the detailed settings for the architecture and placement comparisons in Section 4.2 and the multilingual model in Section 4.3. Each optimizer advances its own learning-rate schedule; discriminator updates begin in the adversarial phase. C.2 TTS training and sampling Table C2 provides the shared settings for the TTS comparison in Section 6.2. The temporal backbone and text embeddings are initialized from pretrained Qwen3-0.6B weights; the local Transformer and codec-specific embeddings and prediction heads are newly initialized. Losses are computed only on the target sequence, excluding the conditioning prefix and padding. Cross-entropy is averaged over valid positions within each batch for each head, and the resulting head losses are averaged with equal weights. For evaluation (Sections 6.26.3), codebook tokens and durations are sampled with temperature 0.8, top-p 0.95, and top-k 50; repetition penalty of 1.1 applies only to codebook tokens, using the history of the corresponding codebook. Continuation or stop is sampled from the binary distribution at temperature 1.0, without truncation or repetition penalty.
